steps.title: Remember
steps.body: Every point you make needs evidence. "Show, don't just tell." A quotation shows exactly what the writer did.

steps.title: Technique
steps.body: Introduce the quotation with your own words, then quote only the key words. The quotation becomes part of YOUR sentence.

steps.title: Recommended
steps.body: 5-8 key quotations per major text. Choose quotations that can be used for multiple themes or characters. Quality over quantity.

steps.title: Top Tip
steps.body: In closed-book exams, quotation recall under time pressure is critical. Spend the first 5 minutes of planning time jotting down the 3-4 quotations you will use. This prevents you forgetting key quotes mid-essay and ensures every paragraph has evidence ready before you start writing.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: What makes a good quotation for analysis? | What's the difference between dropping and embedding a quotation? | How many quotations should you memorise per text?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Good quotations are: rich in language techniques (metaphor, imagery), significant to character/theme, concise (short enough to analyse word by word), and flexible (can be used for multiple points). | Dropping: quotation stands alone as separate sentence. Embedding: quotation is part of your sentence structure. Embedded quotations flow naturally and show stronger integration. | Recommended 5-8 key quotations per text. Choose quotations that work for multiple themes/characters. Quality over quantity - better to know a few well than many poorly.
